query: What is the difference between a circuit-breaker and a disconnector, and which IEC standard specifies the ratings and tests for the circuit-breaker?
answer:
## Circuit-breaker vs. disconnector

These are two distinct **mechanical switching devices**, sitting side-by-side in the same IEC 60617-7 "Switchgear and controlgear" section [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear].

**Circuit-breaker** — symbol **[07-13-05]** (FR *Disjoncteur*). A circuit-breaker is a switching device capable of **making, carrying and breaking currents under normal conditions, and also making, carrying for a specified time, and breaking currents under abnormal conditions such as short-circuit** [circuit-breaker] ([iec-56] 3.102.3 / IEV 441-14-20). What sets it apart from a plain switch is precisely its **short-circuit interrupting duty** — it is built to interrupt fault currents, with a continuous-current [main-contact] and an [arcing-contact] that takes the arc during interruption.

**Disconnector (isolator)** — symbol **[07-13-06]** (FR *Sectionneur*). A disconnector is an **isolating device**: its job is to provide a visible/positive isolating gap in the circuit for safety, not to interrupt load or fault current. It is essentially an **off-load** device. The contrast is made explicit by the neighbouring symbols in the same table: the **switch-disconnector** [07-13-08] is labelled the "on-load isolating switch" (FR *Interrupteur-sectionneur*), i.e. you need that variant to break load current — the plain disconnector does not [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear]. The section also offers a two-way disconnector with centre-off isolating position [07-13-07] and a manually-operated disconnector with blocking device [07-13-10].

**In short:** the circuit-breaker is the active protective device that interrupts normal *and* short-circuit currents; the disconnector is a passive isolating device that establishes a safe open gap and is operated essentially without load.

## Which standard specifies the circuit-breaker's ratings and tests

**IEC 56 — "High-voltage alternating-current circuit-breakers"** (4th edition, 1987) [iec-56]. It is a *specification* standard (not a symbol dictionary) defining the ratings, design requirements and tests for HV AC circuit-breakers on systems above 1000 V; the device represented by symbol [07-13-05] is exactly the circuit-breaker specified by IEC 56 [iec-56].

- **Ratings → clause 4.** The rated characteristics are the values the breaker is designed and guaranteed to meet — rated voltage [rated-voltage], rated insulation level [rated-insulation-level], rated frequency, rated normal current, rated short-time and peak withstand currents, rated short-circuit breaking and making currents, rated transient recovery voltage, and rated operating sequence [rated-value] ([iec-56] clause 4).
- **Tests → clause 6 (type tests).** These verify a representative breaker meets its ratings: dielectric tests (6.1), radio-interference-voltage tests (6.2), temperature-rise tests (6.3), main-circuit resistance (6.4), short-time/peak withstand tests (6.5), mechanical/environmental tests (6.101), and short-circuit making-and-breaking tests including terminal-fault, short-line-fault and out-of-phase tests (6.102–6.110), plus capacitive and small-inductive switching [type-test].

(Note: the disconnector has no ratings/tests specification within this wiki — IEC 56 governs the circuit-breaker specifically.)

query: Commission a new 24 kV outdoor circuit-breaker on a substation feeder. Verify it can interrupt the maximum three-phase fault current at its terminals and withstand the resulting recovery voltage before the feeder is energised.
answer:
## SOW Analysis — Commissioning a 24 kV outdoor circuit-breaker

### The device, symbol, and governing standard
The equipment is a high-voltage AC **circuit-breaker** — a mechanical switching device that makes, carries and breaks normal currents *and* makes/carries/breaks short-circuit currents, which is precisely what distinguishes it from a plain switch [circuit-breaker]. In IEC 60617 it is drawn as symbol **[07-13-05] "Circuit breaker"** (FR *Disjoncteur*), found in IEC 60617-7 §13 Switchgear and controlgear [07-13-05][60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear].

The ratings, design requirements and tests for this device are specified by **IEC 56 — High-voltage AC circuit-breakers** (4th ed., 1987), which covers breakers for indoor/outdoor installation above 1000 V at 50/60 Hz [iec-56]. Symbol [07-13-05] is the symbol for exactly the device IEC 56 specifies — that is the symbol↔standard link the analysis turns on [iec-56][circuit-breaker].

### Requirement 1 — "Interrupt the maximum three-phase fault current at its terminals"
This is the **rated short-circuit breaking current** duty.

- The rated short-circuit breaking current is the highest short-circuit current the breaker can break, and for three-pole breakers its a.c. component is defined against a **three-phase short-circuit** — matching the SOW's "three-phase fault." It is chosen from the R10 series (…16, 20, **25**, 31.5… kA) and characterised by an a.c. r.m.s. component plus a d.c. percentage [rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]. The relevant verification check at commissioning is that this rating ≥ the system's **prospective current** at the breaker terminals — the current that would flow if the poles were replaced by zero-impedance conductors, i.e. the "maximum fault current" the SOW refers to [prospective-current].
- "**At its terminals**" specifically means a **terminal fault**, governed by IEC 56 §4.101/4.102 — *not* a [short-line-fault]. SLF ratings are only required for breakers ≥ 52 kV with breaking current > 12.5 kA connected to overhead lines, so **at 24 kV the short-line-fault duty does not apply** [short-line-fault].
- Capability is proven by the **short-circuit making-and-breaking test**: the breaker must make and break the specified three-phase currents from 10 %–100 % of rated at rated voltage (single-phase at U/√3 added only for earthed-neutral/single-pole use) [short-circuit-test][making-and-breaking-capacity]. This is executed as the five standardised **Test-duties Nos. 1–5** (10/30/60/100 %, with duty 4 the full sequence at 100 % break + 100 % make) [test-duty], to the prescribed **rated operating sequence** (e.g. O–t–CO–t′–CO) [rated-operating-sequence], following the **test procedure** (§6.105) and **test quantities** (§6.104) [short-circuit-test-procedure][short-circuit-test-quantities]. These are **type tests** on a representative breaker, not site tests [type-test].
- Note the closely-coupled **making** duty: commissioning/closing onto a possible fault is bounded by the **rated short-circuit making current** = 2.5× (50 Hz) / 2.6× (60 Hz) the breaking-current a.c. component, equal to the rated peak withstand current [rated-short-circuit-making-current].

### Requirement 2 — "Withstand the resulting recovery voltage"
This maps to the **recovery voltage** and, specifically, the **transient recovery voltage (TRV)**.

- After current interruption, the **recovery voltage** appears across the pole in two stages: the transient (TRV) period, then the power-frequency recovery voltage [recovery-voltage]. If it rises faster than the gap recovers dielectric strength, you get a reignition or restrike [recovery-voltage].
- The breaker's **rated TRV for terminal faults** is the limiting envelope of prospective TRV it can handle, tied to the rated short-circuit breaking current [transient-recovery-voltage]. At **24 kV (< 100 kV) a two-parameter envelope (u_c, t₃)** applies — e.g. the tabulated 12 kV point is u_c = 20.6 kV, t₃ = 60 µs (first-pole-to-clear factor 1.5); a 24 kV breaker falls in this two-parameter regime [transient-recovery-voltage]. **ITRV may be neglected below 25 kA**, which will typically cover a distribution-class 24 kV feeder breaker [transient-recovery-voltage]. The test quantities also fix the power-frequency recovery voltage at U/√3 × first-pole factor, held ≥ 0.1 s [short-circuit-test-quantities].
- The 24 kV **rated voltage** is the reference that fixes the power-frequency recovery voltage, the rated insulation level, and the standard TRV values [rated-voltage].

### Requirement 3 — "24 kV outdoor" (dielectric/environmental qualification)
- **Outdoor** installation engages the **external insulation** — air clearances and solid-insulation surfaces exposed to atmosphere, pollution and humidity; it is generally self-restoring [external-insulation].
- Its withstand capability is the **rated insulation level** (power-frequency + lightning-impulse withstand to earth, between poles, and across the open break), coordinated with the 24 kV rated voltage per Table I (≤ 72.5 kV) [rated-insulation-level][rated-voltage].

### Advisory note (commissioning vs. type test)
The SOW asks to "verify before energising." The interrupting and recovery-voltage capabilities are established by **IEC 56 type tests / certification of the rated values**, not by site short-circuit testing [type-test]. The commissioning verification is therefore a **rating-adequacy check**: confirm the unit's certified (a) rated short-circuit breaking current ≥ the calculated prospective three-phase fault current at the feeder terminals [rated-short-circuit-breaking-current][prospective-current]; (b) rated terminal-fault TRV envelope ≥ the system's prospective TRV [transient-recovery-voltage]; and (c) 24 kV rated voltage / insulation level and outdoor (external-insulation) suitability for the site [rated-voltage][rated-insulation-level][external-insulation].

query: Specify a 36 kV circuit-breaker dedicated to switching a shunt capacitor bank and energising no-load overhead lines, such that no switching overvoltages arise from restrikes.
answer:
## Engineering Standards Analysis — 36 kV restrike-free circuit-breaker for capacitor-bank and no-load line switching

### Governing standard & symbol
The device falls entirely under **IEC 56, *High-voltage AC circuit-breakers*** (4th ed., 1987), which governs making/carrying/breaking duties for breakers on systems >1000 V [iec-56]. The graphical symbol is **[07-13-05]** "Circuit breaker" in [60617-7]; the IEC 56 circuit-breaker is precisely what that symbol represents [circuit-breaker]. A circuit-breaker is defined at 3.102.3 [circuit-breaker].

### The defining requirement — "restrike-free"
The SOW's "no switching overvoltages from restrikes" maps directly to one IEC 56 classification:

- A **restrike** is a resumption of current **a quarter-cycle or more** after current zero (3.105.47) — a *late* dielectric failure occurring after the recovery voltage has built up, which is what generates escalating overvoltages in capacitive switching [restrike]. Contrast a **reignition** (<¼ cycle, 3.105.46), which is far less onerous because the recovery voltage is still low [reignition].
- A **restrike-free circuit-breaker** (3.102.12) is one that interrupts **without restrike during the capacitive-current breaking test duties** [restrike-free-circuit-breaker]. This is the exact attribute the SOW demands — and it is a *performance* class, not a construction type: any medium (vacuum, SF₆, etc.) qualifies if it passes the tests [restrike-free-circuit-breaker].

Physics behind the hazard: after a capacitive current zero, trapped charge holds the load side near peak, leaving up to **twice peak voltage** across the gap as a one-cosine [recovery-voltage] rebuilds [capacitive-current-switching-test][recovery-voltage]. A restrike at that point causes the overvoltage escalation the SOW must avoid [restrike].

### Base ratings to fix
- **Rated voltage U_r = 36 kV** — highest r.m.s. phase-to-phase service voltage (4.1, a standard Series I value) [rated-voltage].
- **Rated insulation level** — since 36 kV ≤ 72.5 kV, **Table I applies** (rated power-frequency and lightning-impulse withstand to earth, between poles, and across the open gap) (4.2.1) [rated-insulation-level]. Adequate across-the-open-gap withstand is what physically prevents restrikes.

### Applicable switching (capacitive) duties — and why
**Shunt capacitor bank** → assign one of two breaking ratings depending on system layout:
- **[rated-single-capacitor-bank-breaking-current]** (4.107) — if *no* other shunt banks are on the source side; inrush limited by supply inductance only.
- **[rated-back-to-back-capacitor-bank-breaking-current]** (4.110) — if parallel banks sit on the source side, giving high-frequency inrush on closing.
- If back-to-back, **[rated-capacitor-bank-inrush-making-current]** (4.111) becomes **mandatory** — a *making* duty for the 2–5 kHz inrush surge that stresses the closing contacts [rated-capacitor-bank-inrush-making-current]. For both, the principal interruption hazard is restrike → voltage escalation [rated-single-capacitor-bank-breaking-current][rated-back-to-back-capacitor-bank-breaking-current].

**Energising/de-energising no-load overhead lines** → **[rated-line-charging-breaking-current]** (4.107): the duty of switching an unloaded line, interrupting its distributed charging current against a one-cosine recovery voltage; the chief concern is restrike [rated-line-charging-breaking-current].

> ⚠ **36 kV nuance worth flagging in the spec.** IEC 56 confines the standard line-charging rating to *three-pole breakers ≥ 72.5 kV*, and explicitly states line-charging breaking below 72.5 kV is "generally unnecessary" (6.111.1) [rated-line-charging-breaking-current][capacitive-current-switching-test]. The SOW still requires no-load line switching at 36 kV, so this duty (and its restrike-free verification) must be **assigned by special agreement with the manufacturer** rather than read off the standard tables. (Note also that for *cables*, the analogous [rated-cable-charging-breaking-current] is deemed unnecessary ≤24 kV, 4.108 — not binding here but the same logic.)

In all cases the manufacturer states the **maximum permissible switching overvoltages** (suggested values, Table IX) that must not be exceeded [rated-line-charging-breaking-current][rated-single-capacitor-bank-breaking-current].

### Mandatory verification
Compliance is demonstrated by the **[capacitive-current-switching-test]** (clause 6.111), required for any breaker assigned a line-charging, single- or back-to-back capacitor-bank breaking, or capacitor-bank inrush making current [capacitive-current-switching-test]:
- Laboratory proof of the line-charging rating is **valid only if the breaker is restrike-free** (6.111.2).
- Four test-duty series (Table XIX) at 20–40 % and ≥100 % of rated capacitive current, 10 three-phase (or 12 single-phase) tests each (6.111.8).
- **Acceptance = no restrikes**, with trapped-charge voltage held 0.3 s (6.111.9) [capacitive-current-switching-test].

This is governed by the recovery-voltage / [transient-recovery-voltage] envelopes that define how fast the gap must recover (4.102) [transient-recovery-voltage][recovery-voltage].

### Technology note (selection guidance)
"Restrike-free" is performance-defined, so specify by *test result*, not construction [restrike-free-circuit-breaker]. At 36 kV (medium voltage), the **[vacuum-circuit-breaker]** is dominant and well-suited: sealed vacuum interrupter, rapid dielectric recovery, extinction at first current zero — favourable margins against capacitive restrike [vacuum-circuit-breaker]. The **[sf6-circuit-breaker]**, with SF₆'s electronegative rapid recovery, is the other restrike-free-capable option [sf6-circuit-breaker]. Either can be cited provided it passes 6.111 without restrike.

### One-line spec summary
*36 kV, Table I insulation level, restrike-free (IEC 56 §3.102.12) circuit-breaker, with assigned single- or back-to-back capacitor-bank breaking current (§4.107/4.110) — plus capacitor-bank inrush making current (§4.111) if back-to-back — and a line-charging breaking current (§4.107) assigned by special agreement; all verified restrike-free by the capacitive-current switching test (§6.111) within the manufacturer's Table IX maximum permissible switching overvoltages.*

query: Overhaul a flameproof (Ex d) 3.3 kV induction motor: rewind the stator, recondition the sleeve bearings, and return it to its certified condition for the hazardous area.
answer:
## Standards Analysis — Overhaul of a flameproof (Ex d) 3.3 kV induction motor

### Governing standard
This SOW is a **repair/overhaul of explosion-protected apparatus**, so it is governed by **IEC 79-19** *Repair and overhaul of Ex electrical apparatus*, not by the IEC 60617 symbol parts (those only supply the diagram symbols) [iec-79-19]. IEC 79-19 is organised as a matrix of *type-of-protection × component*; you read down the column for your protection type and across the rows for each component you touch [iec-79-19].

The work is an **overhaul** — restoring an in-service machine to *fully serviceable condition*, more thorough than maintenance and distinct from modification [overhaul][serviceable-condition]. "Return it to its certified condition" is the defining constraint: the work must **not invalidate the explosion-protection certification** [iec-79-19][certification].

### Applicable clause set: type of protection "d" → IEC 79-19 **clause 3**
Flameproof "d" relies on an **enclosure that contains an internal explosion and stops flame transmission via tightly controlled flame paths/gaps**; those gaps "must not be reclaimed beyond spec" [type-of-protection-d]. All sub-requirements below are the **.2 (repair/overhaul)** and **.3 (reclamation)** rows of clause 3.

### Task-by-task mapping

**1. Rewind the stator** — the electrical construction drives explosion safety, so this is the most tightly governed task:
- **Winding data (3.2.6):** obtain original winding data, *preferably from the manufacturer*; otherwise use **copy-winding** techniques to reproduce the original exactly [windings][copy-winding]. Rating must **not** be increased even if a better insulation system is fitted, without manufacturer reference [windings].
- **Insulation (3.2.4):** replace with the **same or a superior class** (IEC 85 — e.g. class E → class F), but a superior class does **not** license any rating increase without the manufacturer [insulation].
- **Stator core (3.3.4):** any skimmed or damaged stator core must be **flux-tested** to confirm no hot spots that could infringe the temperature class or damage windings; if the core is skimmed, the increased air gap must not alter pressure-piling or raise surface temperatures beyond the temperature class [rotors-and-stators].

**2. Recondition the sleeve bearings** — this is **reclamation** (restoring dimensions by adding/removing material) [reclamation]:
- **Sleeve-bearing surfaces (3.3.3):** may be reclaimed by **electroplating or metal spraying** [sleeve-bearings].
- **Shafts & bearing housings (3.3.2):** ⚠️ critical for Ex d — these **include flameproof joints** (the shaft/spigot gaps are flame paths). They may be reclaimed by metal spraying/sleeving (welding with care), but **any subsequent machining must be to the flamepath dimensions specified in the apparatus standard/certification** [shafts-and-housings]. Reconditioning bearings cannot be treated as a purely mechanical job — the journal/housing dimensions are part of the explosion protection.

**3. Return to certified condition (the Ex d enclosure & paperwork)**
- **Enclosure reassembly (3.2.1 / 3.3.1):** prefer new manufacturer parts; on re-assembly, **flameproof joints must comply with the standard/certification**. Reclaimed enclosure parts may be reused only if they pass the applicable over-pressure test [enclosures].
- **Threaded holes / flameproof joint faces (3.3.1.2–.3):** damaged fastener threads and corroded joint faces may be reclaimed/machined **only after consulting the manufacturer** and **without altering the joint gap, flange dimensions or surface finish** below the permitted level [threaded-holes-for-fasteners].
- **Certification check:** study the certificate first — a **"X" suffix** on the certificate number signals **special conditions of use** that must be reviewed before repair/overhaul [certificate-references][certification].
- **Responsibilities:** the **user** selects a competent **repairer** and supplies the work scope, certification and special conditions, then verifies the protection is intact on return; the **repairer** must hold the required training/documentation/facilities; the **manufacturer** is the reference point for winding data and any rating question [user][repairer][manufacturer].

### Post-repair testing (clause 3.2.6.3)
After the rewind, with the machine preferably assembled: **winding-resistance measurement** (balanced across the three phases), an **insulation-resistance test** (≥500 V d.c.; not less than ~20 MΩ at 20 °C for a complete rewind up to 660 V), a **high-voltage test**, and an **energized rated-voltage check**; as a rotating machine it additionally needs a **full-speed run** (noise/vibration) and a **locked-rotor reduced-voltage full-load** current/phase-balance test (see IEC 34) [testing-after-repair]. Note: at **3.3 kV this is a high-voltage machine**, and the clause flags that high-voltage (and non-cage) machines **may require further tests** [testing-after-repair].

### Boundary / cautions
- Keep the job a **repair/overhaul**, not a **modification**: if the rewind changed the **voltage, speed or rating**, it becomes a modification under **3.4.4** (manufacturer reference required; magnetic loading, current densities, losses, creepage/clearance and temperature class all constrained; **rating plate updated**) — and a modification can **invalidate certification** [modification][windings]. The SOW's "return to certified condition" means like-for-like, so stay within clause 3.2/3.3.
- A faulty die-cast cage rotor would have to be **replaced with a new manufacturer rotor** (bar-wound cages may be rewound to identical spec, kept tight in the slots) — relevant if rotor damage is found [windings][rotors-and-stators].

### Relevant IEC 60617 symbols (for diagrams/documentation)
- **[06-08-01]** Induction motor, three-phase, squirrel cage — or **[06-08-03]** three-phase wound-rotor, depending on the actual machine; see the family at [60617-6-08-examples-of-induction-asynchronous].
- **[02-01-04]** Envelope/enclosure element — used to depict the flameproof enclosure on diagrams [02-01-04].

## SOW Analysis — 11 kV Outgoing Feeder Bay

**Scope:** Document a bay with four primary devices — isolator, circuit-breaker, current transformer, voltmeter — with the circuit-breaker rated to the busbar fault level. Below: the IEC 60617 graphical symbol for each device, and the IEC 56 rating chain that pins down "rated for the busbar fault level."

### 1. Device symbols (IEC 60617 "Graphical symbols for diagrams")

| SOW device | Symbol | Page | Section / Part | Why it applies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Isolator** | Disconnector (isolator) *Sectionneur* | **[07-13-06]** | [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear] · [60617-7] | "Isolator" is the British term for the IEC **disconnector** — the off-load isolating device drawn in switchgear section 13 [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear]. If the bay isolator must switch load, the on-load variant **switch-disconnector** [07-13-08] applies instead; a lockable version exists as [07-13-10]. |
| **Circuit-breaker** | Circuit breaker *Disjoncteur* | **[07-13-05]** | [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear] · [60617-7] | The dedicated CB symbol [07-13-05], sitting beside the disconnector in the same section [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear]. It denotes the [circuit-breaker] concept — the switching device able to make/carry/break short-circuit current, the device specified by [iec-56]. |
| **Current transformer** | Current transformer (general) *Transformateur de courant* | **[06-09-10]** (Form 1) / [06-09-11] (Form 2) | [60617-6-09-general-symbols-transformers-and] · [60617-6] | The general single-CT symbol for the feeder metering/protection core. If multiple secondary cores (metering + protection) are needed, use the multi-core examples [06-13-02], [06-13-04], or the 3-tapping [06-13-06] from [60617-6-13-examples-of-measuring-transformers]. |
| **Voltmeter** | Voltmeter *Voltmètre* | **[08-02-01]** | [60617-8-02-examples-of-indicating-instruments] · [60617-8] | The indicating-instrument symbol [08-02-01] for the bay's voltage indication. |

**Gap to flag:** at 11 kV a voltmeter is not connected directly to the primary — it is fed through a **voltage transformer** [06-13-01], which the SOW does not list. If busbar/feeder voltage indication is intended, add a VT [06-13-01] to the bay schedule. Likewise the CT [06-09-10] normally drives an **ammeter** [08-02-02 family]; the SOW pairs the CT with a voltmeter, so confirm whether the CT feeds a protection relay rather than an instrument.

### 2. "Rated for the busbar fault level" — the IEC 56 rating chain

The circuit-breaker is specified by **[iec-56]** (High-voltage AC circuit-breakers, for systems >1000 V — 11 kV qualifies). "Rated for the busbar fault level" maps onto a linked set of rated characteristics:

- **Reference voltage** — the 11 kV system sets the **rated voltage** Uᵣ (highest r.m.s. phase-to-phase voltage), which fixes the recovery voltage and insulation level [rated-voltage].
- **The fault level itself** — the busbar fault level is the **rated short-circuit breaking current**: the highest short-circuit current the CB can interrupt, chosen from the R10 series (…16, 20, 25, 31.5, 40 kA…) [rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]. The station's prospective fault current at the busbar [prospective-current] must not exceed this value.
- **Carrying the fault** — the CB (and the bay) must also withstand the fault thermally and mechanically: the **rated short-time withstand current** equals the breaking current [rated-short-time-withstand-current], and the **rated peak withstand current** expresses the electrodynamic peak [rated-peak-withstand-current].
- **Closing onto the fault** — the **rated short-circuit making current** = **2.5×** (50 Hz) the breaking-current a.c. component, and equals the peak withstand current [rated-short-circuit-making-current].

**Practical reading:** "rated for the busbar fault level" means selecting one R10 value (e.g. 25 kA) as the **rated short-circuit breaking current** ≥ the calculated busbar prospective fault current, at Uᵣ ≥ 12 kV (the standard rating above 11 kV), with short-time-withstand = breaking current and making/peak = 2.5× that value following automatically. The isolator [07-13-06] and the CT [06-09-10] in the same bay must carry the same short-time/peak withstand levels.

## SOW Analysis: Repairing a combined Ex e + Ex i enclosure to certified condition

### 1. Governing standard
This is not a symbol-dictionary question — it is a **repair-procedure** question, governed by **IEC 79-19** "Repair and overhaul of electrical apparatus for explosive gas atmospheres" [iec-79-19]. That standard is organised as a **matrix**: one clause per type of protection × a row per component. Your SOW lands on **two protection-type clauses at once, inside one shared housing**, which is the defining complication here.

- **Increased safety "e"** → requirements in **clause 6** [type-of-protection-e]
- **Intrinsic safety "i"** → requirements in **clause 4** [type-of-protection-i]

Within each clause: **.2** = repair & overhaul, **.3** = reclamation, **.4** = modification [iec-79-19].

### 2. First, classify the work (definitions decide which rules bind)
"Repair … and restore to certified condition" most likely means **[repair]** (restore a damaged/worn item to a serviceable condition, 2.2) and possibly **[overhaul]** (restore to *fully* serviceable, 2.2.3). Confirm it is **not** a **[modification]** — any change to material, fit, form or function (2.2.7) invalidates the certified design and must instead follow the .4 modification rules with reference to the [manufacturer]. **"Restore to certified condition" = the [serviceable-condition] test (2.2.1):** a replacement/reclaimed part may be used only "without prejudice to the … explosion-protection aspects … with due regard to the certification requirements."

**Action before touching anything:** read the certificate. If the certificate number carries the **suffix "X"**, there are **special conditions of use** that must be studied before repair/overhaul/modification [certificate-references]. Confirm responsibilities: the **[user]** issues instructions and supplies the certification documents; the **[repairer]** must hold the training, documentation and facilities of clause 2.6 [repairer][user][manufacturer].

### 3. The Ex e terminal box (clause 6)
A terminal box has no windings, so the post-rewind test battery does **not** apply; the live components are the enclosure, its entries and its terminals:

- **[enclosures] (6.2.1):** preserve the **degree of protection (IP) and temperature classification on the certification label**; meet impact-test requirements; use only manufacturer-specified finishes.
- **[cable-and-conduit-entries] (6.2.2):** glands/entries must preserve a **minimum IP54 per IEC 529**. No additional entries except under modification rules (6.4.2).
- **[terminations] (6.2.3) — the heart of an Ex e box:** creepage/clearance distances and the insulation's **comparative tracking index (CTI)** are specified in the certification documents, so **replacement terminals should come from the manufacturer or be used on his advice**; loose-lead terminations must comply with the certification documents. No modification without reference to the manufacturer (6.4.3).
- **[internal-wiring] (6.2.5):** renewed internal connections must be **no inferior** electrically/thermally/mechanically and **no smaller in cross-section** than the original.

### 4. The Ex i instrument circuit (clause 4)
For "i", safety lives in the circuit's energy limiting and conductor separation, **not** in the enclosure:

- **[internal-wiring] (4.2.12) — critical:** certain **inter-conductor distances and segregation are safety-critical**; disturbed IS wiring must be **put back in its original position**, and damaged insulation/screens/sheaths/double-insulation replaced with equivalent material in the **same configuration**.

- **[terminations] (4.2.3):** replacement terminals should be the same type; any alternative must meet creepage (per CTI)/clearance for the max voltage **and the separation that prevents inadvertent cross-connection**.
- **[enclosures] (4.2.1) / [cable-and-conduit-entries] (4.2.2):** where an enclosure/entry is present, repair **must not reduce its degree of protection**.

### 5. ⚠️ The combined-enclosure synthesis (the real risk)
Because both circuits share **one enclosure**, the two clauses interact — this is the point a generic repair will miss:

- The **50 mm separation between IS and non-IS circuits** and the IS segregation rules (4.2.12 / 4.2.14) must survive **any** work done on the Ex e side. Re-routing or re-terminating the Ex e conductors must not encroach on the Ex i spacing.

- The enclosure's IP/temperature class must be re-established for the "e" requirement (6.2.1–6.2.2) *and* not be relied upon for the "i" circuit's safety — both conditions apply simultaneously.

### 6. Verification before return to the hazardous area
- **Ex i mandatory test (4.2.16):** before re-installation, apply **500 V a.c. (50–60 Hz) for 1 minute between the IS-circuit terminals and the enclosure** to check insulation (may be omitted only if the enclosure is insulating and one side is galvanically bonded for safety) — see [testing-after-repair].
- **Ex e:** verify restored creepage/clearance, CTI-compliant terminal insulation, and IP54 entries against the certification label. (The winding-repair test regime of 6.2.6.3 is not triggered by terminal-box work.)
- The [user] must satisfy itself on return that explosion protection is intact [user].

### 7. Relevant 60617 symbols (graph cross-links)
- **[02-01-04]** — envelope/enclosure symbol; note that "special protective features … may be drawn to by a note," which is exactly how an Ex enclosure would be annotated.
- **[03-02-02]** — terminal symbol; the node for both the Ex e and Ex i termination work.

### Bottom line
Both repairs are governed by **IEC 79-19**, clause **6** ("e") and clause **4** ("i"), with the **enclosure, entries and terminations** rows applying to the box and the **internal-wiring + encapsulated-parts** rows applying to the instrument circuit. Treat it as **repair to [serviceable-condition]**, not modification; **read the certificate (check "X")** first; **buy manufacturer parts** for "e" terminations and "i" barriers; **preserve IS segregation/50 mm separation** while working the "e" side; and finish with the **500 V/1-min IS insulation test** before re-energising.

## Analysis of Circuit-Breaker Specification for Shunt Capacitor Bank and No-Load Overhead Line Switching

This analysis identifies relevant standards, clauses, and symbols for a 36 kV circuit-breaker required for switching shunt capacitor banks and energising no-load overhead lines, with a critical requirement for no switching overvoltages from restrikes.

### 1. Applicable Standard

The primary standard governing high-voltage alternating-current circuit-breakers is **IEC 56 — High-voltage AC circuit-breakers** (4th edition, 1987) [iec-56]. This specification standard defines ratings, design requirements, and tests for AC circuit-breakers with rated voltages above 1000 V, directly applicable to a 36 kV device.

### 2. Circuit-Breaker General Requirements

A [[circuit-breaker]] is defined as a mechanical switching device capable of making, carrying, and breaking currents under normal and specified abnormal (e.g., short-circuit) conditions [circuit-breaker]. The SOW requires a circuit-breaker suitable for 36 kV systems, which falls within the scope of IEC 56. Key components include the [[main-circuit]], [[main-contact]], and [[arcing-contact]] within each [[pole]] [circuit-breaker].

### 3. Specific Application Requirements and Clauses

#### 3.1 Switching a Shunt Capacitor Bank

For switching shunt capacitor banks, the following clauses from IEC 56 are critical:

*   **Rated single capacitor bank breaking current** [iec-56]: Clause 4.107 defines the maximum capacitor current the circuit-breaker must be capable of breaking at its rated voltage without exceeding permissible switching overvoltages. This directly addresses the breaking duty for a single shunt capacitor bank.
*   **Rated capacitor bank inrush making current** [iec-56]: Clause 4.111 specifies the peak current the circuit-breaker must make when energising a capacitor bank, accounting for the high-amplitude, high-frequency current surge during closing.

#### 3.2 Energising No-Load Overhead Lines

For energising (and de-energising) no-load overhead lines, the circuit-breaker must handle the associated capacitive currents:

*   **Rated line-charging breaking current** [iec-56]: Clause 4.107 defines the maximum line-charging (capacitive) current the circuit-breaker shall be capable of breaking at its rated voltage. While specification is typically for rated voltages at or above 72.5 kV, the underlying capacitive duty is still present at 36 kV, and the breaker must be capable of interrupting such currents without issues.
*   **Rated cable-charging breaking current** [iec-56]: Clause 4.108 defines the equivalent for unloaded insulated cables, representing a similar capacitive breaking duty.

#### 3.3 Mitigation of Switching Overvoltages from Restrikes

The requirement that "no switching overvoltages arise from restrikes" is paramount:

*   **Restrike** [iec-56]: A restrike is a resumption of current between contacts occurring a quarter of a cycle or more after current zero [restrike]. Restrikes are particularly problematic in capacitive switching (capacitor banks, no-load lines) as they can lead to escalating and damaging overvoltages.
*   **Restrike-free circuit-breaker** [iec-56]: The circuit-breaker must be classified as a [[restrike-free-circuit-breaker]], meaning it interrupts without restrike during the capacitive current-breaking test duties specified in IEC 56 [restrike-free-circuit-breaker].
*   **Capacitive current switching test** [iec-56]: Clause 6.111 of IEC 56 details the [[capacitive-current-switching-test]]. This test verifies restrike-free performance when interrupting capacitive currents. Acceptance requires no restrikes and that the trapped-charge voltage is held for 0.3 seconds [capacitive-current-switching-test]. This test is crucial for verifying the specified performance.

### 4. Relevant Graphical Symbols (IEC 60617-7)

IEC 60617-7 outlines graphical symbols for switchgear, controlgear, and protective devices [60617-7]. For a circuit-breaker, the following symbols are relevant:

*   **Circuit breaker symbol:** [[07-13-05]] represents a circuit-breaker in diagrams [60617-7-13-switchgear-and-controlgear].

*   **Older Circuit-breaker symbol:** [[07-A2-08]] is an older, alternative symbol for a circuit-breaker [60617-7-A2-appendix-a-older-symbols].

### Conclusion

To meet the SOW, the 36 kV circuit-breaker must comply with IEC 56, particularly regarding its ability to handle capacitive currents from shunt capacitor banks and no-load overhead lines. Crucially, it must be a "restrike-free circuit-breaker," confirmed by successful completion of the "capacitive current switching test" as per IEC 56, clause 6.111, to prevent switching overvoltages. 1.  **General Overhaul Principles**:
    *   The term "overhaul" [overhaul] is defined in **IEC 79-19 clause 2.2.3** as an action to restore an apparatus that has been in service to a **fully serviceable condition**, which is more thorough than routine maintenance. Furthermore, any rewinding undertaken for a different voltage or speed **requires manufacturer reference** (**IEC 79-19 clause 3.4.4**). This is to ensure that magnetic loading, current densities, and losses are not increased; new creepage and clearance distances are established; the temperature class is respected; and the rating plate is updated accordingly.

    *   **Sleeve bearings** [sleeve-bearings]: The reclamation of sleeve-bearing surfaces for flameproof enclosures is addressed in **IEC 79-19 clause 3.3.3**. It explicitly states that sleeve-bearing surfaces may be reclaimed by electroplating or metal spraying.

The overhaul of the flameproof (Ex d) 3.3 kV induction motor demands strict adherence to **IEC 79-19** [iec-79-19], especially **clause 3**, to ensure the integrity of its explosion protection. This includes meticulously following guidelines for stator rewinding (with emphasis on original data, flux testing, and manufacturer consultation for any changes in rating or operating parameters) and approved methods for reconditioning sleeve bearings (e.g., electroplating or metal spraying). # SOW Analysis — Commissioning a 24 kV Outdoor Circuit-Breaker

## Device & symbol
The equipment is a **circuit-breaker**: a mechanical switching device able to make, carry and break currents under normal conditions *and* to make, carry-for-a-specified-time and break short-circuit currents — the short-circuit interrupting duty is exactly what distinguishes it from a plain switch [circuit-breaker]. On a single-line feeder diagram it is drawn as IEC 60617-7 symbol **[07-13-05] "Circuit breaker"** (section 13, switchgear and controlgear) [07-13-05].

## Governing standard
The applicable specification is **IEC 56 — High-voltage AC circuit-breakers** (4th ed., 1987), which covers indoor/outdoor breakers on systems above 1000 V at 50/60 Hz and defines all ratings, design requirements and tests. Symbol [07-13-05] is the graphical representation of precisely the device IEC 56 specifies [iec-56]. The two SOW verifications map onto two of its rated characteristics and the clause-6 test programme.

## The 24 kV rating
Rated voltage U_r is the highest r.m.s. phase-to-phase voltage the breaker is designed for; **24 kV is a standard Series I value** (3.6 / 7.2 / 12 / 17.5 / **24** / 36 / 52 / 72.5 kV) [rated-voltage]. This single number is the anchor: it fixes the power-frequency recovery voltage in every breaking duty, the rated insulation level, and the standard TRV envelope — so both SOW requirements are referenced back to U_r = 24 kV [rated-voltage].

## Requirement 1 — "interrupt the maximum three-phase fault current at its terminals"
- The relevant rating is the **rated short-circuit breaking current** — the highest short-circuit current the breaker can break, with the a.c. component referring to a **three-phase short-circuit** for three-pole breakers (IEC 56 4.101). Selected from the R10 series (…16, 20, 25, **31.5**, 40… kA) [rated-short-circuit-breaking-current].
- The "maximum fault current at its terminals" is the system's **prospective current** — what would flow if each pole were replaced by a zero-impedance link, set by source/circuit impedance alone [prospective-current]. **Verification = the breaker's rated short-circuit breaking current must be ≥ the feeder's prospective three-phase fault current at 24 kV.**
- This capability is *proven by type test*, not on the live feeder: the **short-circuit (making & breaking) test** of IEC 56 6.102 demonstrates making/breaking from 10 %→100 % of rated, run as the five standardised **test-duties** (No. 1 @10 %, No. 2 @30 %, No. 3 @60 %, **No. 4 @100 % breaking + 100 % making**, No. 5 @100 % asymmetrical) [short-circuit-test][test-duty]. Quantities and procedure are fixed by 6.104/6.105, executed at the **rated operating sequence** (O–t–CO–t′–CO) [short-circuit-test-quantities][short-circuit-test-procedure][rated-operating-sequence].
- A closely related duty: when the breaker *closes onto* a fault, the **rated short-circuit making current** (peak; 2.5× the a.c. r.m.s. at 50 Hz) governs — relevant because commissioning energises the feeder [rated-short-circuit-making-current].

## Requirement 2 — "withstand the resulting recovery voltage"
- **Recovery voltage** is the voltage appearing across an open pole after current interruption, in two stages: the **transient recovery voltage (TRV)** immediately after current-zero, then the power-frequency recovery voltage. If it rises faster than the gap recovers dielectric strength, you get a reignition/restrike — i.e. a failed interruption [recovery-voltage].
- The rated **TRV** for terminal faults is a standardised envelope: for U_r < 100 kV a two-parameter (u_c, t₃) curve (e.g. at 12 kV: u_c ≈ 20.6 kV, t₃ = 60 µs). 24 kV sits in this sub-100 kV / two-parameter band [transient-recovery-voltage].
- **Key engineering point:** Requirements 1 and 2 are *not separate tests* — they are one coupled rated duty. The rated short-circuit breaking current is *defined* as the current the breaker can break **in a circuit whose power-frequency recovery voltage corresponds to U_r and whose TRV equals the rated value of 4.102** [rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]. The short-circuit test therefore applies the prospective TRV and a power-frequency recovery voltage held ≥95 % for ≥0.1 s while breaking the fault current [short-circuit-test-quantities]. **Verification = the feeder's prospective TRV must lie under the breaker's rated TRV envelope at the same time the fault current is broken.**

## How to actually "verify before the feeder is energised"
This is the most important advisory caveat. You **cannot** break the maximum fault current on the installed unit during commissioning. The SOW's two verifications are satisfied by **type tests** (IEC 56 clause 6), performed once on a representative breaker to prove the *design* meets its rated characteristics — as distinct from routine tests run on every unit [type-test]. Practically:
1. Confirm the breaker's type-test certificate shows **rated short-circuit breaking current ≥ feeder prospective fault current** and **rated TRV envelope ≥ feeder prospective TRV**, both at U_r = 24 kV.
2. On-site commissioning before energising is then **routine/mechanical and dielectric checks** (insulation, timing, operating mechanism), not an actual fault-breaking test.

## Scope boundaries (deliberately excluded)
- **Short-line fault** is a *separate* breaking duty for a fault some distance *down the line*; the SOW says "**at its terminals**," so the terminal-fault duty above is the correct one, not SLF.
- **Single-phase short-circuit test** (at U/√3) applies to earthed-neutral / single-pole use; secondary to the three-phase terminal-fault duty the SOW specifies [short-circuit-test].
- `standard-rated-voltages` (read and ruled out) is the **surge-arrester** page (IEC 99-4), not the circuit-breaker rated-voltage list — not applicable here.
- "Outdoor" implies the rated insulation level / dielectric type test also matters for siting, but it is outside the fault-interruption + recovery-voltage scope of this SOW.

# Specifying a 36 kV restrike-free capacitor/line switching circuit-breaker

## 1. Governing documents & graphical symbol
- **Standard:** The device is a high-voltage AC **circuit-breaker** (rated voltage > 1000 V), so it is governed by **IEC 56, 4th ed. 1987** — ratings, design requirements and type tests [iec-56]. Apply it together with **Amendment 1 (1992-11)** [iec-56-amendment-1], which is the source for the capacitive-switching procedure you'll rely on.
- **Symbol:** On diagrams the device is drawn as **[07-13-05] "Circuit breaker"** (IEC 60617-7, §13 switchgear) — this is exactly the device IEC 56 specifies [iec-56][07-13-05][circuit-breaker].

## 2. Voltage class and insulation
- **36 kV is a standard Series I rated voltage** (the ≤72.5 kV list: 3.6…24; **36**; 52; 72.5 kV), so it is a legitimate U_r under IEC 56 §4.1 [rated-voltage].
- Because 36 kV ≤ 72.5 kV, the **rated insulation level comes from Table I** (§4.2) — rated power-frequency and lightning-impulse withstand to earth, between poles and across the open break [rated-insulation-level]. Verified by the **dielectric test** (§6.1) [dielectric-test]. This matters here: restrike-free capacitive switching depends on the open-gap dielectric strength out-recovering the recovery voltage.

## 3. The two switching duties → which capacitive ratings apply
Both stated duties are **capacitive** switching, the onerous case (after current zero the trapped charge leaves up to ~2× peak voltage across the gap) [capacitive-current-switching-test].

**(a) Shunt capacitor bank** — assign one of:
- **Rated single capacitor-bank breaking current (§4.107)** if no other shunt banks sit on the source side [rated-single-capacitor-bank-breaking-current]; **or**
- **Rated back-to-back capacitor-bank breaking current (§4.110)** if parallel banks are present on the source side [rated-back-to-back-capacitor-bank-breaking-current]. If back-to-back, you **must also** specify the **rated capacitor-bank inrush making current (§4.111)** — mandatory whenever a back-to-back breaking current is assigned; the parallel banks discharge a 2–5 kHz surge into the bank being energised [rated-capacitor-bank-inrush-making-current].
  - *Decision the SOW must resolve:* single vs. back-to-back arrangement, because it changes both the breaking rating clause and whether an inrush making rating is required.

**(b) Energising/de-energising no-load overhead lines** — this is the **rated line-charging breaking current (§4.107)**: switching an unloaded overhead line, where a one-cosine recovery voltage builds as the trapped line charge holds the line side near peak [rated-line-charging-breaking-current].
- ⚠️ **Key caveat / standards gap:** IEC 56 confines the line-charging rating to **three-pole breakers for lines ≥ 72.5 kV**, with standard Table VII values starting at 72.5 kV; capacitive line-charging tests **below 72.5 kV are "generally unnecessary"** per §6.111.1 [rated-line-charging-breaking-current][capacitive-current-switching-test]. At **36 kV this falls below the standard threshold**, so a line-charging rating and its test must be specified **by special agreement / on request**, not taken from the standard tables. (If the unloaded circuit were cable rather than overhead line, note cable-charging is likewise deemed unnecessary at ≤ 24 kV but *would* apply at 36 kV under §4.108 [rated-cable-charging-breaking-current].)

## 4. The core requirement — "no switching overvoltages from restrikes"
This is a precise IEC 56 term: specify a **restrike-free circuit-breaker (§3.102.12)** — one that interrupts **without restrike** during the capacitive test duties [restrike-free-circuit-breaker].
- A **restrike** is current resuming **a quarter-cycle or more after current zero** — late enough that the recovery voltage has built up, so it drives the escalating overvoltages you want to exclude [restrike][recovery-voltage]. (Contrast a **reignition**, < quarter-cycle, low recovery voltage, far less onerous — not the failure mode of concern here [reignition].)
- "Restrike-free" is a **performance classification, not a construction type** — any medium can qualify if it passes the capacitive tests [restrike-free-circuit-breaker].

## 5. Verification — the capacitive current switching test (IEC 56 §6.111)
This is the type test that proves the restrike-free claim and validates the ratings above [capacitive-current-switching-test][type-test]:
- Applies to any breaker assigned a line-charging, single- or back-to-back capacitor-bank breaking current, or inrush making current (§6.111.1).
- **Laboratory verification of the breaking ratings is valid only if the breaker is restrike-free** (§6.111.2) — i.e. a single restrike invalidates the rating.
- Four **test-duty** series (Table XIX) at 20–40% and ≥100% of rated capacitive current, 10 three-phase (or 12 single-phase) tests each, using two supply circuits A and B [test-duty].
- **Acceptance: no restrikes**, with the trapped-charge voltage held for 0.3 s.
- **Amendment 1** added an alternative **§6.111.9 "Tests with specified TRV"** (prospective-recovery-voltage envelopes, new Figures 32a/32b and Table XX) — a permissible test route [iec-56-amendment-1].

## 6. Technology choice
At 36 kV (medium voltage), the practical restrike-free candidates are the **vacuum circuit-breaker** (dominant in MV switchgear; rapid dielectric recovery in the sealed bottle) [vacuum-circuit-breaker] or the **SF₆ circuit-breaker** (electronegative gas, fast recovery) [sf6-circuit-breaker]. Either can be specified provided it passes §6.111 restrike-free.

## 7. Remaining ratings to complete the specification
Round out the IEC 56 nameplate so the breaker is fully defined, not only for the capacitive duty:
- **Rated normal (continuous) current** from the R10 series (400…6300 A), §4.4 [rated-normal-current];
- **Rated short-circuit breaking & making current**, **rated TRV** (for 36 kV a two-parameter (u_c, t₃) envelope, first-pole factor 1.5) and **rated operating sequence**, proven via the basic short-circuit **test-duties** and **making/breaking capacity** [transient-recovery-voltage][test-duty][making-and-breaking-capacity];
- These short-circuit duties are independent of the capacitive duty but are part of any complete circuit-breaker spec.

## 8. Complementary overvoltage limiting (optional, defence-in-depth)
The primary control per the SOW is restrike-free interruption itself. As a backstop against any residual switching transient, a **surge arrester** can be applied to clamp overvoltages [surge-arrester]; its graphical symbols sit in IEC 60617-7 §22 (e.g. the **gap [07-22-01]**, and the lightning-arrester symbol 07-22-03). This is supplementary, not a substitute for specifying the breaker as restrike-free.

---

**Bottom line:** Specify a **36 kV (Series I) restrike-free circuit-breaker** to **IEC 56 (1987) + Amd 1**, symbol [07-13-05]; assign a **single or back-to-back capacitor-bank breaking current** (§4.107/§4.110, plus mandatory **inrush making current** §4.111 if back-to-back) and — by special agreement, since 36 kV is below the standard's 72.5 kV line-charging threshold — a **line-charging breaking current** (§4.107); require **restrike-free performance (§3.102.12)** proven by the **capacitive current switching test (§6.111)** with the **no-restrike** acceptance criterion.

## Standards Analysis — Overhaul of a flameproof (Ex d) 3.3 kV induction motor

### Governing standard
The whole job is the **overhaul/repair of explosion-protected apparatus**, so the controlling document is **[iec-79-19]** — *Repair and overhaul of Ex electrical apparatus*. Because the motor is flameproof "**d**", the applicable clause set is its **clause 3** (type "d"). The flameproof *construction* baseline it must be restored to is **[iec-79-1]** (Construction & verification of flameproof enclosures); note the wiki's local copy of 79-1 is front-matter only, so the actionable "d" repair detail lives in 79-19 clause 3. Surface-temperature limits referenced throughout come via **[temperature-classes-t1-t6]**.

The job is **[repair]/[overhaul]** (restore to original design), **not [modification]** — this distinction drives everything below.

### SOW task → applicable clauses / concepts

**1. Frame the job: "overhaul … return to certified condition"**
- **[overhaul]** = restore an in-service apparatus to *fully* serviceable condition (79-19 §2.2.3); **[serviceable-condition]** (§2.2.1) means usable without prejudice to explosion-protection, with due regard to certification.
- **[certification]** (§2.2.11) and **[certificate-references]** (§2.2.12): if the certificate number carries the **"X" suffix** (special conditions of use), the certification documents *must* be studied before any work.
- Responsibilities: **[user]** issues instructions and supplies the certification/special conditions (§2.5); **[repairer]** must hold the competence, documentation and facilities (§2.6); **[manufacturer]** reference is required for winding data and any rating change.

**2. Rewind the stator**
- **[windings]** (§3.2.6): obtain original winding data preferably from the manufacturer, else use **[copy-winding]** (§2.2.13) techniques. **The rating shall not be increased.**
- **[insulation]** (§3.2.4): replacement insulation may be the same as or superior class per **IEC 85** (e.g. class E → class F), but a superior class does **not** license any rating increase without manufacturer reference.
- **[rotors-and-stators]** (§3.3.4): if the stator core is skimmed/damaged, **flux-test** it for hot spots that could infringe the temperature class or damage windings; any air-gap increase must not alter pressure-piling characteristics or raise external surface temperature beyond the **T-class**.
- **[testing-after-repair]** (§3.2.6.3): after rewind — winding-resistance (3-phase balanced), insulation-resistance test (≥500 V d.c.), high-voltage test, energised rated-voltage check; plus a **full-speed run** and a **locked-rotor reduced-voltage full-load test** (see **IEC 34**). ⚠️ The "≥20 MΩ / up to 660 V" insulation figure is for LV rewinds — at **3.3 kV this is a high-voltage machine**, and the clause explicitly notes high-voltage machines may need *further* tests.

**3. Recondition the sleeve bearings**
- **[sleeve-bearings]** (§3.3.3): plain bearing surfaces may be **reclaimed by electroplating or metal spraying** ([reclamation], §2.2.6).
- **[shafts-and-housings]** (§3.3.2): shafts and bearing housings — **including flameproof joints** — may be reclaimed by metal spraying/sleeving (welding with care), but any subsequent machining **must be back to the flamepath dimensions** specified in the apparatus standard/certification. This is the safety-critical link: a bearing-housing surface is often part of the flameproof flame path.

**4. Preserve the flameproof ("d") integrity — implicit in "certified condition"**
- **[enclosures]** (§3.2.1, §3.3.1): re-assembly must keep flameproof joints compliant; reclaimed parts only if they pass the over-pressure test.
- **[threaded-holes-for-fasteners]** (§3.3.1.2/.3): damaged joint faces/threads reclaimed only after consulting the manufacturer and without altering joint gap, flange dimensions or surface finish.
- **[cable-and-conduit-entries]** (§3.2.2): entries must still conform to the standard/certification after overhaul; do not add entries or change indirect→direct entry without manufacturer reference (§3.4.2).

### Key flags / boundaries
- **Repair vs modification:** A straight like-for-like rewind is repair. **Any change of voltage, speed or rating → [modification] (§3.4.4)** and requires manufacturer reference (magnetic loading/current densities/losses not increased, new creepage/clearance, T-class respected, **rating plate updated**). Keep the 3.3 kV rating and speed unchanged to stay within "repair."
- **Temperature class is the running constraint** ([temperature-classes-t1-t6]): rewind insulation choice, stator skimming and bearing/air-gap work must none of them raise the maximum surface temperature past the certified T-class.

### Relevant IEC 60617 symbols (for diagrams/documentation)
- **[06-08-01]** — Induction motor, three-phase, squirrel cage (the most likely 3.3 kV machine); alt. **[06-08-03]** wound-rotor, in section **[60617-6-08-examples-of-induction-asynchronous]**.
- **[06-04-01]** — Machine, general symbol (asterisk → **M** for motor).
- Stator winding: **[06-02-07]** three-phase star winding (and 06-03-01).

### Bottom line
This is a **clause-3 ("d") overhaul under IEC 79-19**, restoring the motor to its **IEC 79-1 flameproof construction** and certified rating. The two SOW tasks are explicitly covered: the **stator rewind** by §3.2.4/§3.2.6 + flux test §3.3.4 + post-repair tests §3.2.6.3, and the **sleeve-bearing reconditioning** by §3.3.3 with the flame-path machining caveat of §3.3.2. To "return to certified condition," do not change rating/voltage/speed (else §3.4.4 modification), use ≥-equivalent insulation (IEC 85) without uprating, protect the T-class throughout, and run the IEC 34 electrical and mechanical tests — having first checked the certificate for an "X" special-conditions suffix.

# SOW Analysis — Repairing a combined Ex e / Ex i enclosure to certified condition

## Governing standard
The whole job is governed by **IEC 79-19, "Repair and overhaul"** [iec-79-19] — the procedure standard for restoring explosion-protected apparatus *without invalidating its certification*. It is organised as a **matrix: type of protection (one clause each) × component**, with sub-clauses `.2` repair & overhaul, `.3` reclamation, `.4` modification [iec-79-19]. Your two protection types map to two clauses:

- **Ex e (increased safety)** → **clause 6** [type-of-protection-e]
- **Ex i (intrinsic safety)** → **clause 4** [type-of-protection-i]

"Restore to certified condition" is the standard's defining objective: every action must leave the apparatus in a **serviceable condition** — usable "without prejudice to the performance or explosion-protection aspects… with due regard to the certification requirements" [serviceable-condition]. Distinguish the four actions up front, because they carry different rules: **repair** (restore a damaged/worn item) [repair], **overhaul** (restore to *fully* serviceable) [overhaul], **reclamation** (restore dimensions by adding/removing material) [reclamation], and **modification** (a design change to material/fit/form/function — which can *invalidate* certification and is allowed only under the `.4` rules) [modification].

## Side 1 — Ex e terminal box (clause 6)
| Component | Requirement to restore certified condition |
|---|---|
| **Enclosure** | Repair/replace only so the **degree of protection (IP) and temperature class on the certification label are preserved**, impact-test requirements met, manufacturer-specified finishes only (6.2.1) [enclosures] |
| **Cable & conduit entries** | Must preserve a **minimum IP54 per IEC 529** (6.2.2); a modified entry must keep the specified type and degree of protection (6.4.2) [cable-and-conduit-entries] |
| **Terminations** | Materials, **creepage/clearance distances and comparative tracking index (CTI)** are fixed by the certification documents → replacement parts come **from the manufacturer or on his advice**; loose-lead terminations must comply with the cert docs (6.2.3); no modification without reference to the manufacturer (6.4.3) [terminations] |
| **Internal wiring** | Renewed connections must be **no worse electrically/thermally/mechanically and no smaller in cross-section** than originally fitted (6.2.5) [internal-wiring] |
| **Encapsulated parts** | Generally **not repairable or reclaimable** — replace as a unit (6.2.8) [encapsulated-parts] |

The decisive characteristics for "e" are creepage/clearance and the temperature class [type-of-protection-e] — so the termination and entry rules above are the heart of this side of the job.

## Side 2 — Ex i instrument circuit (clause 4)
Intrinsic safety is a property of the **circuit's energy**, not the enclosure: no spark or thermal effect under normal-plus-fault conditions may ignite the gas [intrinsically-safe-circuit][type-of-protection-i]. It is also a **system property** — barriers/associated apparatus and cable parameters bound the energy [intrinsically-safe-system] — so repairs must not alter the certified circuit parameters.

| Component | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Internal wiring** | **Critical inter-conductor distances and segregation** — disturbed wiring must be **re-located in its original position**; damaged insulation, screens, sheaths or double insulation replaced by **equivalent material, re-fixed in the same configuration** (4.2.12) [internal-wiring] |
| **Terminations** | Use the **same type** of terminal where possible; any alternative must satisfy creepage (per CTI), clearance, and the **separation needed to avoid inadvertent cross-connection** (4.2.3) [terminations] |
| **Encapsulated parts (safety barriers)** | **Shunt-diode safety barriers are totally encapsulated — no repair**; a replacement must keep the **same safety description, the same U value, and the 50 mm IS/non-IS separation** (4.2.7, 4.2.14) [encapsulated-parts] |
| **Enclosure / entries** | Repairs must **not reduce the IP degree of protection** the enclosure offers (4.2.1, 4.2.2) [enclosures][cable-and-conduit-entries] |
| **Post-repair test** | Before re-installing in the hazardous area, apply **500 V a.c. for 1 minute between the IS terminals and the enclosure** (omit only for an insulating enclosure galvanically bonded to the circuit for safety) (4.2.16) [testing-after-repair] |

Re-verification that the circuit is still intrinsically safe ultimately rests on the IEC 79-11 / **IEC 79-3 spark-test** regime that the "i" certification is built on [iec-79-3] — relevant if the work could affect circuit parameters rather than a like-for-like part swap.

## The critical interaction — *both in one enclosure*
Because the Ex e (non-IS) terminal box and the Ex i (IS) circuit share **one enclosure**, the single most important constraint is **maintaining the IS/non-IS segregation**: keep the **50 mm separation** between intrinsically-safe and non-intrinsically-safe parts, and re-locate any disturbed IS wiring to its **original position** (4.2.12, 4.2.14) [internal-wiring][encapsulated-parts]. A repair that is individually correct on each side can still **invalidate the "i" certification** if the two circuits are brought closer or cross-connected — this is the failure mode to design the work around.

## Restoring "certified condition" — responsibilities & limits (clause 2)
- **Read the certificate first.** A **"X" suffix** on the certificate number means special conditions of use; the certification documents **must be studied before** the apparatus is repaired, overhauled, reclaimed or modified [certificate-references]. Certification itself is the conformity assessment by a recognised authority (or self-certification against recognised standards) [certification].
- **User** holds statutory responsibility for keeping the apparatus serviceable, selects a competent repairer, and issues instructions covering the work, the original certification and any special conditions; on return must satisfy itself the explosion-protection is intact [user].
- **Repairer** (manufacturer, user, or third-party agency) must hold the training, documentation and facilities clause 2.6 requires [repairer].
- **Stay on the repair side of the line.** Keeping like-for-like (manufacturer parts, original dimensions, original insulation/creepage/separation) is *repair/overhaul* and preserves certification. Any change to material/fit/form/function becomes a **modification** — allowed only under 6.4 ("e") / 4.4 ("i") and typically requiring **reference to the manufacturer or certifying authority** [modification].

## Related 60617 symbols (the graph cross-links)
The physical objects in the SOW map to: **[02-01-04]** envelope/enclosure (the box) and **[03-02-02]** terminal (both the Ex e terminals and the IS terminations) [enclosures][terminations][cable-and-conduit-entries].

---

**Bottom line:** treat this as one IEC 79-19 job with two parallel tracks — clause 6 for the Ex e box (preserve IP/temp-class label, IP54 entries, certified creepage/CTI terminations) and clause 4 for the Ex i circuit (original wiring positions, same safety-description barriers, 500 V re-test) — bound by the shared-enclosure 50 mm segregation rule, the certificate (check for "X"), and the repair-vs-modification boundary.

The plain off-load isolator is [07-13-06]. The CT symbols in [60617-6-13-examples-of-measuring-transformers] are all *multi-winding examples*; for a single metering core on a single-line feeder diagram you draw the same construct with one secondary.

### 2. "Circuit-breaker must be rated for the busbar fault level" — the governing standard

The circuit-breaker symbol [07-13-05] connects, via the [circuit-breaker] concept page, to its specification standard **[iec-56]** (High-voltage AC circuit-breakers, 4th ed.) — applicable because the bay is >1000 V AC. "Rated for the busbar fault level" is a chain of IEC 56 clause-4 ratings:

- **Fault level = the prospective short-circuit current at the busbar** — the current that would flow if the breaker poles were replaced by zero-impedance links [prospective-current]; its [prospective-peak-current] sets the asymmetrical peak.
- **Breaking duty** — the breaker's **[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]** (a.c. component from the R10 series 6.3…100 kA) must be **≥ the busbar fault level**, referenced to its [rated-voltage] and the standard TRV.
- **Making duty** — it must be able to close onto the fault: **[rated-short-circuit-making-current]** = 2.5× (50 Hz) the breaking-current a.c. r.m.s. value, and this equals the **[rated-peak-withstand-current]** (electrodynamic stress) [rated-peak-withstand-current].
- **Carry duty** — thermal: **[rated-short-time-withstand-current]** = the breaking current, carried for the **[rated-duration-of-short-circuit]** (standard 1 s, 3 s if longer needed).
- **Continuous duty** (feeder load, not fault) — **[rated-normal-current]** from the R10 series (400, 630, 800 A …), sized to the feeder load.

So a single chosen short-circuit current value (one R10 step) simultaneously fixes the breaking, short-time-withstand, peak-withstand and making ratings — the design action is "pick a breaker whose rated short-circuit current ≥ the calculated busbar fault level."

### 3. The 11 kV figure

11 kV is the *nominal system* voltage; the breaker's **[rated-voltage]** (highest phase-to-phase r.m.s.) is the next standard step above it — **Series I 12 kV** [rated-voltage]. That 12 kV rating in turn fixes the **[rated-insulation-level]** (Table I power-frequency and lightning-impulse withstand) for the bay's dielectric design. (Caution: the [standard-rated-voltages] table in the wiki is the *surge-arrester* series from [iec-99-4], not the circuit-breaker series — use the [rated-voltage] page's Series I list for the breaker.)

### 4. Gaps / out of scope in this wiki
- No dedicated standard page exists for **disconnectors** (IEC 129) or **instrument transformers** (IEC 185/61869) — only their 60617 symbols are catalogued, so isolator and CT ratings can't be sourced from the wiki.
- The **voltmeter** appears only as an indicating-instrument symbol [08-02-01]; the wiki's metrology page [accuracy-class-and-protective-class] covers energy-meter classes (IEC 387), not switchboard voltmeter accuracy, so it is only loosely related.

**Bottom line:** draw the bay with [07-13-06] → [07-13-05] → [06-13-04] → [08-02-01]; specify the circuit-breaker per [iec-56] at 12 kV rated voltage ([rated-voltage]) with a rated short-circuit breaking current ([rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]) selected from the R10 series to equal or exceed the busbar prospective fault current — which automatically sets its making, short-time-withstand and peak-withstand ratings.

query: Commission a new 24 kV outdoor circuit-breaker on a substation feeder. Verify it can interrupt the maximum three-phase fault current at its terminals and withstand the resulting recovery voltage before the feeder is energised.
